title: Yakus v. United States (1944)
summary: Congress may hand an agency the power to fix wartime prices when the statute states its policy and standards clearly enough that Congress, the courts and the public can tell whether the agency has followed them.
notes:
Key line: Only if we could say that there is an absence of standards for the guidance of the Administrator's action, so that it would be impossible in a proper proceeding to ascertain whether the will of Congress has been obeyed, would we be justified in overriding its choice of means for effecting its declared purpose of preventing inflation. (Chief Justice Stone)

Citation: 321 U.S. 414 (1944).

sections.Parties: Petitioners Albert Yakus and Benjamin Rottenberg were Boston wholesale meat dealers. Rottenberg was tried together with associates in a companion case, No. 375. The respondent was the United States, which prosecuted them under the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942. The price ceilings they were charged with breaking had been set by the Price Administrator, who headed the Office of Price Administration, an agency Congress created in January 1942 to hold down prices during the Second World War. The Administrator was not a party, but the validity of his regulation and of the statute that empowered him was the center of the case.
sections.Material Facts: The Emergency Price Control Act of 1942, amended in October 1942, declared a purpose of stabilizing prices and preventing wartime inflation. Section 2(a) let the Administrator fix maximum prices that in his judgment would be generally fair and equitable and would effectuate the purposes of the Act, told him to give due consideration to prices prevailing between October 1 and October 15, 1941, and required him to publish a statement of the considerations behind each regulation. Sections 203 and 204 let anyone subject to a regulation protest to the Administrator within sixty days, with review only in a new Emergency Court of Appeals and then in the Supreme Court; no other court could pass on a regulation's validity. Petitioners sold wholesale cuts of beef above the ceilings in Revised Maximum Price Regulation No. 169 (7 Fed. Reg. 10381). They never filed a protest.
sections.Procedural History: Petitioners were indicted in the United States District Court for Massachusetts for willful violations of sections 4(a) and 205(b) of the Act. The trial court refused to let them attack the validity of Regulation No. 169 and excluded their evidence that the ceilings were unfair. A jury convicted them. The Court of Appeals for the First Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Nos. 374 and 375 to decide whether the Act delegated legislative power unconstitutionally and whether the exclusive protest procedure could bar a validity defense in a criminal case. The Court heard argument on January 7, 1944 and decided the case on March 27, 1944, affirming the convictions by a vote of six to three. Chief Justice Stone wrote for the Court.
sections.Issue: Did the Emergency Price Control Act delegate legislative power to the Price Administrator without adequate standards, in violation of Article I? Could Congress make the protest and Emergency Court of Appeals procedure the only way to challenge a price regulation, so that a defendant charged with violating the regulation could not raise its invalidity as a defense at his criminal trial, without denying due process under the Fifth Amendment or the jury trial rights of the Sixth and Seventh Amendments? The Court also considered whether the sixty-day protest period and the absence of any judicial stay pending review were themselves fair.
sections.Holding: No unconstitutional delegation occurred. Congress fixed the policy, prevention of wartime inflation, and gave standards, fair and equitable prices with attention to October 1941 prices, that are definite enough for Congress, the courts and the public to judge the Administrator's compliance. The exclusive review procedure is valid. Congress may separate the question of a regulation's validity, sent to the Administrator and the Emergency Court, from the question of violation, tried in a criminal court, and petitioners who never used the protest procedure cannot complain that it would have denied them due process. Neither the sixty-day limit nor the lack of a stay was unconstitutional on its face. The jury decided the only factual issue open at trial, so no jury right was lost. Convictions affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Stone began with the difference between legislating and administering. The essentials of the legislative function are the choice of policy and its statement as a binding rule; Congress kept both when it declared the aim of preventing inflation and told the Administrator to fix prices that are fair and equitable in light of October 1941 levels. Finding facts and forming subsidiary policy within that frame is administration, even when it calls for judgment. Congress need not choose the method involving the least delegation; it may prefer flexible standards to a rigid freeze. The Court distinguished Schechter Poultry, where no standards at all existed, and said it would strike down the choice of means only if standards were so absent that a court could not tell whether Congress's will had been obeyed. On procedure, the Court read sections 203 and 204 as exclusive and found nothing in the Constitution that forbids Congress from making violation of a regulation a crime while committing the regulation's validity to a separate tribunal. Petitioners were not required to sell at a loss; they could have stopped selling and protested within sixty days, with the Emergency Court able to admit new evidence and correct any denial of due process. Denial of interlocutory stays is a permissible legislative judgment in an emergency. The Seventh Amendment does not reach equity proceedings in the Emergency Court, and the jury tried the fact of violation.

topics.lrs-s-intelligible-principle: Fair-and-equitable prices, stabilization purposes, and specified price considerations supplied standards that the Court regarded as judicially assessable.
topics.lrs-s-delegation-dimensions: Yakus is the wartime-emergency benchmark for how broad a delegation can be while remaining sufficiently specific.

learning.separateOpinions: Six to three. Justice Roberts dissented alone on the merits, concluding that the Act delegated legislative power without real limits and that the Court had drained Schechter and Panama Refining of meaning. Justice Rutledge, joined by Justice Murphy, agreed with the Court on delegation but dissented on procedure, objecting that a criminal court could be forced to convict a defendant while forbidden to consider whether the regulation he violated was valid.
